youtube.title: The coffee ring | Reality Rulebook Season 2 · Episode 4
youtube.caption:
Why does coffee leave a ring? Not blobs.

The edge of a drying drop is stuck to the paper. Water evaporates from that edge, so water from the middle flows out to replace it, and the flow carries the specks along. In our simple model, about nine in ten specks end up in the ring. Make the specks oval and the ring can vanish.

Season 2 · Episode 4.

Sources
1. Deegan, Bakajin, Dupont, Huber, Nagel, Witten, 'Capillary flow as the cause of ring stains from dried liquid drops', Nature 389, 827 (1997) (search excerpt only, not opened): https://doi.org/10.1038/39827
2. Yunker, Still, Lohr, Yodh, 'Suppression of the coffee-ring effect by shape-dependent capillary interactions', Nature 476, 308 (2011) (search excerpt only, not opened): https://doi.org/10.1038/nature10344
3. OpenStax, University Physics Volume 1, 17.5 Sources of musical sound (for the next episode's teaser; not opened): https://openstax.org/books/university-physics-volume-1/pages/17-5-sources-of-musical-sound
4. Our own simple model of the drying drop (compile.py and scene.mjs; made-up numbers; model-check.md): the numbers in the measure beat come from it: https://github.com/arzateruben22/Claude/tree/claude/physics-s2/films/channels/physics/ep10

Narration: synthetic voice (AI). Animation: code-rendered, no stock footage. The top drop is our own simple model with made-up numbers (drawn in 3-D); the lower drop with oval specks and the mug at the end are illustrations, not simulations.
